A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same feedback neural-network research, with matching authors, core methods, and principal experiments. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material such as v1 Figure S1 to v2 Figure S10.

before.justification: v1 reports original spiral-system simulations, irregular-object trajectory predictions, and quadrotor MPC results in Figures 5–9 and the appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds baseline comparisons, sensitivity and disturbance tests, and an evaluation of adaptation-enhanced feedback.

M1.justification: The original linear feedback, learned neural feedback, cascaded prediction, and training algorithms remain. Appendix A.8 adds an optional AdapFNN variant that updates the neural model's last-layer weights online using an adaptive law while retaining linear feedback, introducing a localized but actual change to inference.

E1.justification: The spiral, irregular-object, and quadrotor task domains remain. Figure S12 adds a distinct spiral scenario in which the latent dynamics change abruptly during a trajectory at t = 7 s, extending evaluation beyond the earlier fixed-parameter uncertainty cases.

E2.justification: The quadrotor comparison in Figure 9 expands from four methods to six. MLP-MPC, attributed to Saviolo and Loianno (2023), and AdapNN-MPC, attributed to Cheng et al. (2019), join the retained Nomi-MPC, Neural-MPC, FB-MPC, and FNN-MPC, substantially strengthening comparison against learned and adaptive alternatives.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce a systematic decay-rate sweep and a timed parameter jump; Appendix A.5.4 specifies matching hidden-layer configurations across the expanded learned-model comparison. The original object-prediction split and horizon, quadrotor training-set size, MPC horizon, and stated flight-test uncertainties remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds empirical validation of the theoretical bound, a 12-case linear-feedback ablation, decay-rate sensitivity, sudden-disturbance robustness, and the adaptive-combination study in Figures S1, S9, S11, S12, and S14. The earlier 12-case neural-feedback analysis is retained as Figure S10, rather than newly introduced. Together, the additions substantially expand component and robustness analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions state six training trials with distinct initial network parameters for Figure 8 and report standard deviations across nine object trajectories in Figure 7. v2 introduces no new repeated-run counts, seed-reporting practices, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Figure 9 changes Nomi-MPC/Neural-MPC/FB-MPC/FNN-MPC RMSEs from 0.450/0.301/0.359/0.173 m to 0.248/0.167/0.203/0.093 m under the same stated test setup, without explaining the numerical replacements. It adds MLP-MPC at 0.182 m and AdapNN-MPC at 0.151 m. Figure S14 reports AdapFNN-MPC at 0.108 m versus FNN-MPC at 0.093 m, and the new appendix analyses supply additional findings.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 and Appendix A.2 revise the state-error bound from gamma/sqrt(2 lambda_min(L) - 1) to gamma/lambda_min(L), supporting positive gains rather than requiring lambda_min(L) > 1/2. v2 also adds discrete-time stability analysis with the condition rho(I - Ts L) < 1, and a new adaptive-feedback theorem and Lyapunov argument in Appendix A.8.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims: feedback corrects learned dynamics, improves generalization while preserving nominal-task accuracy, supports linear convergence analysis and learned nonlinear feedback, and benefits object prediction and quadrotor MPC. The supplementary extension does not redefine these principal contributions.

C2.justification: The conclusion replaces the limitation about horizon-dependent convergence time and transient-performance validation with limitations concerning manual tuning and preliminary validation of neural feedback. New discussions address conservative theoretical bounds, unbounded residuals, the noise-versus-convergence tradeoff, and why last-layer adaptation provides little additional benefit. These substantially revise the paper's qualifications and interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the promise of future code release with stated availability and a code-access link. Appendix A.7 newly reports processor models and training costs, including approximately 30 minutes for 50 quadrotor-training epochs and 10–60 minutes for neural feedback. It also documents controller and drag-coefficient provenance and expanded baseline configurations; these are disclosures rather than established changes to the original experiments.

R1.justification: Section 6.3 introduces substantial positioning against online continual learning, test-time adaptation, and adaptive neural networks, citing works including Ghunaim, Liang, Cheng, O'Connell, Richards, and Patil. Earlier survey passages on neural-ODE variants and other generalization approaches are removed or shortened. The revised discussion distinguishes direct dynamics correction from online weight adaptation and motivates combining them.

P1.justification: Most core exposition and the main section sequence remain. Local revisions clarify variable dimensions, correct the measurement count, rename gain adjustment as an ablation study, rewrite related-work and limitations passages, and organize the expanded appendix into additional subsections. The conference header is also added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to distinguish linear and neural feedback, Figure 9 becomes a wider six-panel comparison with an expanded results table, and Figures 4 and 9 are relocated. Several new appendix figures present convergence, ablation, disturbance, training, and adaptive-variant results. The former Figure S1 is retained and resized as Figure S10; Figure 5's duplicated panel label is corrected.

improvement.justification: The added adaptive and MLP baselines, robustness analyses, tighter original error bound, discrete-time stability condition, and reproducibility information better support the retained method. However, the new Theorem 2 proof does not control the parameter-error component of its Lyapunov function in Equation (32), leaving its claimed reuse of the exponential-convergence argument incomplete. Removing the explicit horizon-dependent transient limitation also loses a useful qualification. These weaknesses temper the net improvement.
